sections.h2: Choosing how to sell in Glenville
sections.html:
Glenville sellers choose among an agent, a private deal and a cash buyer, and the choice sets both the closing speed and the condition buyers expect. The town in Schenectady County takes in the part of the county north of the Mohawk River, including the Village of Scotia.

Glenville is largely a bedroom community for Schenectady and Albany, so a house often sells on location, school district and drive time rather than finishes alone. The named areas are Scotia in the south, Alplaus in the east, Hoffmans along Route 5, West Glenville in the northwest, and East Glenville along NY-50. Stoodley Corners, at Route 50 and Glenridge Road, is the commercial core people call Town Center. Buyers price each area differently, so say which one your house sits in when you ask for offers.

Most Glenville homes are lived in by their owners, and values sit in the mid $250,000s. Roughly 91 percent of residents stayed in the same house for a year, so few homes come up and a new listing gets noticed. Most nearby buyers will be households that want a house in mortgage-friendly condition.

sections.h2: Which route fits a house in rough shape
sections.html:
Deferred repairs point toward cash or a discounted as-is listing. Full retail pricing needs a roof, systems and cosmetics that survive both an inspection and a lender's appraisal.

  • Agent listing: most buyers see it, but you handle showings and post-inspection repair requests, and a stalled loan can push the closing back.
  • Private sale: no commission, though pricing, paperwork and haggling are all yours.
  • Cash offer as-is: few contingencies and a date you choose, at a price typically under a fixed-up listing.

Whatever route you take, Real Property Law section 462 has sellers of one to four family homes hand the buyer a signed property condition disclosure statement before the buyer signs a binding contract. An as-is deal is still allowed. The form asks about flood zones, wetlands, fuel tanks, radon tests, roof age, sump pumps and the septic or sewer system, so gather those answers early.

Unfinished work can hold up a lender or a title search. The Town of Glenville Building Department, in the Municipal Center on Glenridge Road, says a permit is required for new construction, additions, structural changes, decks, fences, finished basements, conversions, swimming pools, demolition, roofing, siding and new windows and doors.

Plan on about 10 days for most permit reviews. Built a deck or finished a basement without a permit? Ask the department what it needs before you list, since the buyer's attorney may bring it up at contract.

  • Pools holding over 24 inches of water, even inflatable and quick-set ones, need a permit and final inspection before use.
  • Homes inside the Village of Scotia may deal with the village's own building office.
  • The Glenville Town Court hears summary proceedings, which is where a landlord's eviction case would go if a tenant occupies the house.

sections.h2: Property tax bills and a sale
sections.html:
Two tax cycles run here, and your attorney will divide each between you and the buyer. Town and county bills are usually mailed by January 1 and carry no penalty through January. The collection window runs through April with a penalty each month: 1.25 percent in February, 2.5 percent in March and 3.75 percent in April. On May 1 the unpaid balance moves to the Schenectady County Commissioner of Finance.

School bills arrive around September 1, stay penalty-free through September, and go to the county on November 1 when unpaid. Whatever remains, penalties included, joins the next January town and county bill, so a missed school payment can hit a bill the buyer expects to be clean. Water rent bills go out by June 1, and unpaid water charges are also carried onto the following January bill.

County and town general charges apply to every parcel in town. Town outside, highway and some other lines apply only to parcels outside the village. Fire district and special district charges depend on the street. A house in Scotia also receives a separate village bill, due in June.

A lower assessment helps only if you file before Grievance Day, which in Glenville is the fourth Tuesday in May. Use the state RP-524 complaint form for the challenge.

The Assessor's Office also handles exemptions for low-income seniors, volunteer firefighters and ambulance workers, plus the STAR program. If you receive STAR on the house, tell your closing attorney, because the benefit is tied to the owner. A seller should close the STAR registration after a sale, and a new owner registers once the house becomes their primary home.

Glenville runs an online request just for sellers. The Public Works water and sewer pages include a Closing Adjustment Request form, and the form asks you to allow 48 hours for the water or sewer closing adjustment to be forwarded to the closing contact. File it as soon as you have a contract date so the buyer's attorney is not waiting on a meter reading.

If the house is on a private well or septic system rather than town service, the disclosure statement still asks about water source, water testing, sewage type, and the date a septic tank was last pumped. A cash buyer will usually ask for the same details.

The deed is recorded with the Schenectady County Clerk, and the county then passes the ownership change to the town for data entry. The paperwork follows New York's standard package: form TP-584 and the Real Property Transfer Report RP-5217, plus state transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of price. Fees differ by county, so ask the Schenectady County Clerk for its current schedule, or ask your closing attorney to quote the total.

  • Confirm the legal owners on the deed match the people signing the contract.
  • Collect any open permit paperwork before the attorney orders the title search.
  • Ask the attorney for the final figure for transfer tax and recording fees in writing.

• The net amount after taxes, payoffs, water charges and recording costs, not just the headline price.
  • Whether the buyer takes the house as is, or asks you to complete repairs after inspection.
  • The closing date, and who covers any gap between contract and closing.
  • Proof of funds, if the offer is cash.
  • Any condition tied to the disclosure statement or a title problem.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Glenville house without making repairs first?
faqs.a: Yes. New York law lets a seller and buyer agree to an as-is sale, but you must still give the buyer a signed property condition disclosure statement before the buyer signs a binding contract. Expect an as-is price below a repaired, staged listing.

faqs.q: Who do I pay property taxes to in Glenville?
faqs.a: Town and county bills are paid to the Glenville Receiver of Taxes in January, with monthly penalties through April. School bills are collected in September, and unpaid bills later move to the Schenectady County Commissioner of Finance.

faqs.q: Does a Scotia address change anything about the sale?
faqs.a: It can. Houses inside the Village of Scotia receive a village tax bill due in June, and the village may have its own building office. Houses elsewhere in Glenville do not get that bill.

faqs.q: How do I get the water and sewer figures for my closing?
faqs.a: Submit the closing adjustment request on the town's Public Works water and sewer pages and allow 48 hours. The result goes to the closing contact you name on the form.

faqs.q: When is Grievance Day in Glenville?
faqs.a: The fourth Tuesday in May. File the state RP-524 form before then if you think your assessment is too high.
